function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run from a script) to finish the task.  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH access, replace the URL with the HTTPS clone URL (`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`).

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick `tree` or `ls -R` to see what’s inside:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (you may see something like this):

```
├── app.js
├── package.json
├── README.md
└── src
    └── index.js
```

* `app.js` – entry point of the Node.js app  
* `package.json` – contains dependencies and start script  
* `src/index.js` – main application logic

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses a lightweight Alpine base.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Copies source after installing deps so Docker cache is reused.  
> * Exposes port 3000 (adjust if your app uses a different port).  

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments**  
> * If you’re pushing the image to a private registry, change `image:` to `your-registry/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add two secrets to the repo settings:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (create one under Docker Hub → Settings → Security → New Access Token).  
> * If you’re using GitHub Container Registry instead, replace the login and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to keep the repo tidy, you can also delete any autogenerated files that aren’t needed (e.g., `node_modules`).

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Result**  
> * The new files are now part of the repo.  
> * On the next push to `main`, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and push the Docker image.  
> * You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify that the workflow ran:

```bash
gh run list --workflow docker-build.yml
```

(Requires the GitHub CLI; otherwise check the Actions tab on GitHub.)

---

That’s it! 🎉  
Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, deployment, or workflow to match your exact environment or CI/CD pipeline.
